p.src: Now Qiao Zhou, who held the office of Grand Astrologer, was well versed in the movements of the heavens. When he learned that Kongming intended once more to take the field, he entered the palace and memorialized to the Latter Ruler: “I am charged with overseeing the Astronomical Observatory, and whether the signs portend disaster or good fortune, I must report them. Recently tens of thousands of birds flew in from the south, plunged into the Han River, and died; this is an inauspicious omen. I have also observed the celestial signs and seen the Kui star enter the domain of Taibai. The ascendant force lies in the north, and it is therefore unfavorable to campaign against Wei. Moreover, all the people of Chengdu have heard cypress trees weeping at night. With calamities and portents of these several kinds, the Prime Minister should hold his ground with caution and must not act rashly.” Kongming replied, “The Former Emperor entrusted his orphaned heir to my weighty care. I must exert myself to the utmost in suppressing the rebels. How could I abandon the great affairs of state because of such groundless portents of disaster?” He then ordered the proper officials to prepare the full sacrificial offering at the temple of Emperor Zhaolie. Weeping, he bowed and made this declaration: “I, Liang, have marched from Qishan five times without gaining a single inch of land; my guilt is far from slight! Now I shall once more command the entire army and again march from Qishan. I swear to exhaust all my strength and devotion, destroy the enemies of Han, and recover the Central Plain, bending myself to the task and giving my all until death alone ends my labors!” When the sacrifice was concluded, he took leave of the Latter Ruler, hastened by night to Hanzhong, and assembled his generals to discuss the campaign. Suddenly a report arrived that Guan Xing had died of illness. Kongming burst into loud weeping, collapsed to the ground, and did not revive for a long while. The generals repeatedly tried to console him. Kongming sighed and said, “Alas for so loyal and righteous a man! Heaven did not grant him long life. On this campaign I am deprived of yet another great general!” A later poet lamented him in verse:

p.src: Now in Wei, because a blue dragon had emerged the previous year from a well at Mopo, the reign era had been changed to Qinglong, “Blue Dragon.” It was now the second month of spring in the second year of Qinglong. A close attendant memorialized, “The frontier officers have sent an urgent report that more than three hundred thousand troops of Shu have divided into five columns and once again marched from Qishan.” The ruler of Wei, Cao Rui, was greatly alarmed. He hastily summoned Sima Yi and said, “The men of Shu have not invaded for three years, but now Zhuge Liang has again marched from Qishan. What are we to do?” Sima Yi replied, “Last night I observed the heavens and saw that the ascendant force of the Central Plain is now at its height, while the Kui star encroaches upon Taibai. This is unfavorable to Western Chuan. Kongming, conceited in his own talent and wisdom, now acts contrary to Heaven; he is merely bringing defeat and destruction upon himself. Trusting in Your Majesty’s abundant good fortune, I shall go and defeat him. I wish to recommend four men to accompany me.” Cao Rui asked, “Whom do you recommend?” Sima Yi replied, “Xiahou Yuan had four sons. The eldest is named Ba, with the courtesy name Zhongquan; the second is named Wei, with the courtesy name Jiquan; the third is named Hui, with the courtesy name Yaquan; and the fourth is named He, with the courtesy name Yiquan. Ba and Wei are highly skilled in archery and horsemanship; Hui and He are well versed in military strategy. All four have long wished to avenge their father. I now recommend Xiahou Ba and Xiahou Wei as the left and right vanguards, and Xiahou Hui and Xiahou He as army marshals, to assist jointly in our military counsels and drive back the army of Shu.” Cao Rui said, “Formerly the imperial son-in-law Xiahou Mao mishandled military affairs and lost a great many soldiers and horses. To this day he is too ashamed to return. Are these four men of the same sort as Mao?” Sima Yi replied, “These four cannot be compared with Mao.” Cao Rui granted his request and appointed Sima Yi Supreme Commander, with authority to employ all officers and soldiers according to their abilities and to mobilize troops from every district. Sima Yi accepted the command, took leave of the court, and departed the capital. Cao Rui also bestowed upon Sima Yi a handwritten edict, which read:

p.src: Sima Yi bowed his head and received the edict. That very day he reached Chang’an, assembled troops from every region, four hundred thousand in all, and encamped them along the banks of the Wei River. He then detached fifty thousand troops to construct nine pontoon bridges across the Wei and ordered the vanguard commanders Xiahou Ba and Xiahou Wei to cross the river and pitch camp. Behind the main camp, he also built a fortified town on the Eastern Plain as a safeguard against unforeseen attack. As Sima Yi was conferring with his generals, a sudden report announced that Guo Huai and Sun Li had come to see him. Sima Yi welcomed them in, and when the formal greetings were over, Guo Huai said, “The entire army of Shu is now at Qishan. If they cross the Wei, ascend the plain, and link up with the northern hills, they will sever the Longxi road. That is greatly to be feared.” Sima Yi replied, “Your words are excellent. You shall take overall command of the troops of Longxi and encamp on the Northern Plain. Dig deep ditches, raise high ramparts, and hold your troops without moving; only when their provisions are exhausted may you attack them.” Guo Huai and Sun Li accepted the order, led their troops away, and made camp.

p.src: Now Kongming had again marched from Qishan and established five great camps, arranged as left, right, center, front, and rear. From the Xie Valley straight back to Jiange, he established another unbroken chain of fourteen great camps, dividing his troops among them in preparation for a prolonged campaign, and each day sent men out on patrol. Suddenly a report came that Guo Huai and Sun Li had led the troops of Longxi to encamp on the Northern Plain. Kongming told his generals, “The Wei troops have encamped on the Northern Plain because they fear I shall seize that route and sever the Longxi road. I shall now make a feigned attack on the Northern Plain while secretly seizing the bank of the Wei. Have more than a hundred wooden rafts made, load them with bundles of straw, and select five thousand experienced boatmen to steer them. I shall attack only the Northern Plain under cover of night, whereupon Sima Yi is certain to lead troops to its rescue. If his army suffers even a slight reverse, I shall first send the rear division across to the opposite bank; then I shall place the front division aboard the rafts, ordering them not to land but to drift downstream to the pontoon bridges, set them alight, and sever them, thereby attacking the enemy from behind. I myself shall lead one force to seize the gate of their forward camp. Once we gain the southern bank of the Wei, advancing the army will be no difficult matter.” The generals obeyed his orders and proceeded accordingly.

p.src: But the patrols had already rushed a report to Sima Yi. Sima Yi summoned his generals and said, “There is a scheme behind Kongming’s arrangements. He will claim to be seizing the Northern Plain, but will drift downstream to burn our pontoon bridges and throw our rear into confusion, while attacking us in front.” He immediately issued orders to Xiahou Ba and Xiahou Wei: “When you hear the battle cries rise from the Northern Plain, lead your troops into the southern hills by the Wei River, wait for the army of Shu to arrive, and strike it.” He also ordered Zhang Hu and Yue Chen to lead two thousand archers and crossbowmen into ambush on the northern bank by the pontoon bridges: “If the troops of Shu come downstream on wooden rafts, shoot at them all together and do not let them approach the bridges.” He then sent orders to Guo Huai and Sun Li: “Kongming will come to the Northern Plain while secretly crossing the Wei. Your camp has only just been established and has few men and horses, so you may conceal them all along the route. If the troops of Shu cross the river in the afternoon, they will certainly attack you around dusk. Pretend defeat and flee; the troops of Shu will surely pursue. Then all of you are to shoot them with bows and crossbows. I shall advance by both water and land. If the main force of Shu arrives, watch for my signal and strike.” When all these orders had been issued, he commanded his two sons, Sima Shi and Sima Zhao, to lead troops in support of the forward camp. Sima Yi himself led one force to the relief of the Northern Plain.

p.src: Now Kongming ordered Wei Yan and Ma Dai to lead troops across the Wei and attack the Northern Plain; Wu Ban and Wu Yi to lead the raft-borne troops to burn the pontoon bridges; Wang Ping and Zhang Yi to form the first division, Jiang Wei and Ma Zhong the middle division, and Liao Hua and Zhang Yi the rear division. Thus divided into three columns, they went to attack the Wei army’s landward camp beside the river. At noon that day the troops left the main camp, all crossed the Wei, formed their battle array, and advanced slowly. By the time Wei Yan and Ma Dai drew near the Northern Plain, dusk had already fallen. Sun Li’s scouts sighted them, and he at once abandoned the camp and fled. Wei Yan realized that preparations had been made and was urgently withdrawing his troops when tremendous battle cries erupted on every side: Sima Yi attacked from the left and Guo Huai from the right, their two forces closing in. Wei Yan and Ma Dai fought desperately to break through, but more than half the troops of Shu fell into the river, while the survivors found every road of escape barred. Fortunately, Wu Yi’s troops charged in, rescued the routed soldiers, brought them across the river, and held the enemy at bay. Wu Ban sent half his troops to pole the rafts downstream and burn the pontoon bridges, but Zhang Hu and Yue Chen checked them from the bank with a storm of arrows. Wu Ban was struck by an arrow, fell into the water, and died. The remaining troops leapt into the water to save their lives, and all the wooden rafts were seized by the soldiers of Wei.

p.src: At this time, Wang Ping and Zhang Yi, unaware that the forces at Beiyuan had been defeated, hastened straight to the Wei camp. It was already the second watch when they heard shouts rising on every side. Wang Ping said to Zhang Yi, “Our troops have attacked Beiyuan, but we do not yet know whether they have won or lost. The camp south of the Wei River lies before us, yet why is there not a single Wei soldier in sight? Can it be that Sima Yi has learned of our plan and made preparations beforehand? Let us wait until flames rise from the floating bridge before advancing.” The two reined in their troops. Suddenly a mounted messenger came from behind and reported, “The Chancellor orders the army to return at once. Both the forces at Beiyuan and those at the floating bridge have been defeated.” Wang Ping and Zhang Yi were greatly alarmed. Just as they hurriedly began to withdraw, the Wei troops swept around behind them. At the report of a cannon, they charged all at once, while flames soared into the sky. Wang Ping and Zhang Yi led their men to meet the attack, and the two armies fought in a confused melee. Wang Ping and Zhang Yi fought their way out with all their strength, but more than half the Shu troops were killed or wounded. Kongming returned to the main camp at Qishan and gathered the surviving troops. More than ten thousand men had been lost, leaving him deeply troubled.

p.src: When Sun Quan had finished reading, he was delighted and said to Fei Yi, “We have long wished to raise an army, but have had no opportunity to coordinate with Kongming. Now that his letter has arrived, We shall raise an army this very day, advance through Juchao, and seize Xincheng from Wei. We shall also order Lu Xun, Zhuge Jin, and the others to station troops at Jiangxia and Miankou and seize Xiangyang. Sun Shao, Zhang Cheng, and the others shall march from Guangling to seize Huaiyang and the surrounding places. The three armies, totaling three hundred thousand men, shall advance together on the appointed day.” Fei Yi bowed in gratitude and said, “If this is indeed done, the Central Plain will soon fall of itself!” Sun Quan gave a banquet in Fei Yi’s honor. During the feast, Sun Quan asked, “Who serves as the foremost attacker against the enemy in the Chancellor’s army?” Fei Yi replied, “Wei Yan is foremost.” Sun Quan laughed and said, “That man has courage to spare, but his heart is not upright. If Kongming were gone one day, he would surely bring disaster. Can it be that Kongming does not know this?” Fei Yi said, “Your Majesty’s words are entirely just. When I return, I shall report these words to Kongming at once.” He then took leave of Sun Quan and returned to Qishan. Meeting Kongming, he reported in full that the ruler of Wu was raising a great army of three hundred thousand, would personally lead the expedition, and would advance along three routes. Kongming then asked, “Did the ruler of Wu say anything else?” Fei Yi told him what Sun Quan had said about Wei Yan. Kongming sighed and said, “He is truly an enlightened ruler! It is not that I do not understand this man. I employ him only because I value his courage.” Fei Yi said, “The Chancellor should make arrangements for him early.” Kongming replied, “I have my own way of dealing with him.” Fei Yi took leave of Kongming and returned to Chengdu.

p.src: As Kongming was discussing the next advance with his generals, a report suddenly came that a Wei commander had arrived to surrender. Kongming summoned the man and questioned him. He replied, “I am Zheng Wen, a deputy general of Wei. Recently Qin Lang and I jointly commanded troops under Sima Yi’s orders. But Sima Yi, showing private favoritism, promoted Qin Lang to General of the Vanguard while treating me like worthless grass. Resenting this injustice, I have come expressly to surrender to the Chancellor. I beg you to accept me into your service.” Before he had finished speaking, someone reported that Qin Lang had led troops outside the camp and was challenging Zheng Wen to single combat. Kongming asked, “How does this man’s skill at arms compare with yours?” Zheng Wen replied, “I shall behead him on the spot.” Kongming said, “Only if you first kill Qin Lang shall I cease to doubt you.” Zheng Wen gladly mounted his horse, rode out of the camp, and engaged Qin Lang. Kongming himself went out of the camp to watch. Qin Lang leveled his spear and shouted abuse: “You traitorous wretch! You stole my warhorse and came here—return it at once!” With that, he charged straight at Zheng Wen. Zheng Wen spurred his horse forward and met him with whirling blade. In a single exchange, he struck Qin Lang from his horse and killed him. The Wei soldiers fled in all directions. Zheng Wen carried the severed head into the camp.

p.src: Kongming returned to his tent and took his seat. Summoning Zheng Wen before him, he suddenly flew into a rage and ordered the attendants to drag him out and behead him. Zheng Wen cried, “I have committed no crime!” Kongming said, “I knew Qin Lang in the past. The man you have just slain was not Qin Lang at all. How dare you deceive me!” Zheng Wen bowed and confessed, “That man was in fact Qin Lang’s younger brother, Qin Ming.” Kongming laughed and said, “Sima Yi sent you here under a false surrender to work some scheme from within. How could you possibly deceive me? Unless you tell me the truth, you will certainly be beheaded!” Zheng Wen had no choice but to admit that his surrender was indeed a ruse, and tearfully begged for his life. Kongming said, “Since you wish to live, write a letter telling Sima Yi to come in person and raid our camp. Then I shall spare your life. If Sima Yi is captured, the achievement will be yours, and I shall grant you high office.” Zheng Wen had no choice but to write a letter and present it to Kongming. Kongming ordered Zheng Wen to be taken away under guard. Fan Jian asked, “How did the Chancellor know that this man’s surrender was false?” Kongming replied, “Sima Yi does not employ men lightly. If he promoted Qin Lang to General of the Vanguard, Qin Lang must have possessed exceptional martial skill. Yet the man who crossed weapons with Zheng Wen today was killed by him in a single exchange; therefore he could not have been Qin Lang. That is how I knew it was a deception.” All present bowed in admiration.

p.src: Now Sima Yi, having read Zheng Wen's letter, wished to lead his two sons and a great army in a raid upon the Shu camp. His eldest son, Sima Shi, remonstrated: “Father, why would you venture personally into perilous ground on the strength of a mere scrap of paper? If some mishap should occur, what then? It would be better to send another general ahead and have you follow in support.” Sima Yi accepted his counsel and ordered Qin Lang to take ten thousand troops to raid the Shu camp, while he himself led a force in support. That night, during the first watch, the breeze was fresh and the moon shone brightly; but as the second watch approached, dark clouds suddenly closed in from every side, and black vapors filled the sky until nothing could be seen even at arm's length. Sima Yi rejoiced greatly and cried, “Heaven is granting me success!” Thereupon every man put a gag in his mouth and every horse was bridled to silence, and they drove swiftly forward. Qin Lang led the van, charging with ten thousand troops straight into the Shu camp, but not a single person was to be seen. Realizing that he had fallen into a trap, Qin Lang hastily ordered a retreat. Torches flared on every side, and battle cries shook the earth; from the left came Wang Ping and Zhang Yi, and from the right Ma Dai and Ma Zhong, their two forces attacking at once. Qin Lang fought desperately but could not break free. Behind him, Sima Yi saw flames soaring above the Shu camp and heard unceasing shouts, but, not knowing whether the Wei troops had won or lost, he thought only of hastening his supporting force and charged toward the blaze. Suddenly a great shout arose; drums and horns thundered to the heavens, and firecrackers shook the ground; Wei Yan charged out on the left and Jiang Wei on the right. The Wei army was utterly defeated; eight or nine men in ten were wounded, and the survivors fled in all directions. By then the ten thousand troops led by Qin Lang were completely surrounded by the Shu army, whose arrows flew like locusts. Qin Lang perished amid the mêlée. Sima Yi led his defeated troops back into their own camp.

p.src: After the third watch, the sky cleared once more. From the hilltop, Kongming sounded the gong to recall his troops. In fact, the dark clouds that had gathered during the second watch had been raised by Kongming through the arts of Dunjia; after his troops had withdrawn, the sky cleared because he had commanded the Six Ding and Six Jia spirits to sweep the drifting clouds away. Kongming returned victorious to camp, ordered Zheng Wen beheaded, and then deliberated on a plan to seize the lands south of the Wei River. Each day he sent troops to challenge the enemy, but the Wei army refused to come out and engage them. Kongming himself rode in his small carriage and surveyed the terrain east and west along the Wei River before Mount Qi. Presently he came to the mouth of a valley shaped like a gourd, whose interior could hold more than a thousand men; farther in, two mountains converged upon another hollow that could contain four or five hundred, while two encircling mountains at the rear left passage for only one man and one horse at a time. Kongming was delighted by what he saw and asked the local guide, “What is this valley called?” The man replied, “It is called Shangfang Valley, and is also known as Gourd Valley.” Returning to his tent, Kongming summoned the junior generals Du Rui and Hu Zhong and whispered a secret plan into their ears. He ordered more than a thousand craftsmen attached to the army assembled in Gourd Valley to manufacture wooden oxen and gliding horses for use, and commanded Ma Dai to guard the valley mouth with five hundred troops. Kongming charged Ma Dai: “None of the craftsmen are to be allowed out, and no outsiders are to be admitted. I shall come personally from time to time to inspect the work. My plan to capture Sima Yi depends entirely upon this undertaking. On no account must word of it leak out.” Ma Dai received his orders and departed. Du Rui, Hu Zhong, and the others supervised the craftsmen in the valley as they manufactured the devices according to the prescribed method. Kongming came in person each day to give instructions.

These oxen and horses require neither water nor fodder and can transport supplies without ceasing, day or night.” All were astonished and said, “From ancient times to the present, we have never heard of such things as wooden oxen and gliding horses. p.src: Now while Sima Yi was sunk in anxious gloom, a scout suddenly reported: “The Shu army is using wooden oxen and gliding horses to transport grain and fodder. The men suffer little toil, and the oxen and horses consume no fodder.” Sima Yi was greatly alarmed and said, “The reason I have held fast and refused battle is that their provisions could not be kept supplied; I meant to wait for them to perish of their own accord. Now that they employ this method, they must be planning to remain for a long time and have no thought of withdrawing. What are we to do?” He urgently summoned Zhang Hu and Yue Chen and instructed them: “Each of you is to take five hundred troops and slip out by the narrow path through Xie Valley. Wait until the Shu troops have driven all their wooden oxen and gliding horses past, then charge out together. Do not seize too many; take only three or five and return.” The two obeyed, each leading five hundred troops disguised as Shu soldiers. By night they stole along the narrow path and lay in ambush in the valley; sure enough, they saw Gao Xiang approaching with his troops, guiding the wooden oxen and gliding horses. Just as the last of them were about to pass, the ambushers on both sides raised a clamor and charged out together. Caught unprepared, the Shu troops abandoned several of the devices, and Zhang Hu and Yue Chen joyfully drove them back to their own camp. When Sima Yi examined them, he found that they advanced and retreated as though alive. Delighted, he said, “If you can use this method, do you suppose that I cannot?” He ordered more than a hundred skilled craftsmen to dismantle the devices before him, then instructed them to manufacture identical wooden oxen and gliding horses according to the measurements of every part—their length, breadth, thickness, and thinness. In less than half a month, more than two thousand were completed. Constructed by the same principles as Kongming's, they too could travel; he then ordered Cen Wei, General Who Guards the Distant Lands, to lead a thousand troops and guide the wooden oxen and gliding horses to Longxi, bringing back grain and fodder in an unceasing stream. Every officer and soldier in the Wei camp rejoiced.

p.src: Meanwhile, the Wei general Cen Wei was leading his troops as they drove the wooden oxen and flowing horses, laden with grain. While they were on their way, word suddenly came that soldiers ahead were patrolling the grain convoy. Cen Wei sent men to scout, and when they proved to be Wei soldiers, he put his mind at ease and continued onward. The two forces joined together. All at once, tremendous battle cries erupted, and the Shu soldiers attacked from within the ranks, shouting, “Here stands Wang Ping, great general of Shu!” The Wei soldiers were caught completely unprepared, and more than half were slain by the troops of Shu. Cen Wei led the defeated remnants in resistance, but Wang Ping cut him down with a single stroke; all the rest scattered in rout. Wang Ping led his troops back, driving away all the wooden oxen and flowing horses. The defeated soldiers fled at full speed and carried the news into the Northern Plain camp. When Guo Huai heard that the army’s provisions had been seized, he hastily led his troops to the rescue. Wang Ping ordered his soldiers to twist back the tongues of the wooden oxen and flowing horses. They abandoned them all on the road and retreated while fighting. Guo Huai ordered his men not to pursue for the moment, but merely to drive the wooden oxen and flowing horses back. The soldiers all tried to drive them on, but how could they make them move? Guo Huai was filled with bewilderment. Just as he was at a loss, drums and horns suddenly resounded to the heavens and battle cries arose on every side. Two forces came charging from separate directions: they were Wei Yan and Jiang Wei. Wang Ping also turned his troops back to the attack. Attacked from three sides, Guo Huai suffered a crushing defeat and fled. Wang Ping ordered the soldiers to twist the tongues of the oxen and horses back again, then drive them onward. Seeing this, Guo Huai was just about to turn his troops around and pursue once more when smoke and clouds suddenly billowed up behind the mountain. A band of divine soldiers surged forth, every one of them holding a banner and sword and bearing a grotesque appearance. Driving the wooden oxen and flowing horses before them, they swept away as swiftly as the wind. Guo Huai cried out in terror, “The gods must surely be aiding them!” At the sight, every soldier was struck with fear and awe, and none dared give chase.

Wang Ping ordered the soldiers to twist the tongues of the oxen and horses back again, then drive them onward.

Seeing this, Guo Huai was just about to turn his troops around and pursue once more when smoke and clouds suddenly billowed up behind the mountain. A band of divine soldiers surged forth, every one of them holding a banner and sword and bearing a grotesque appearance. Driving the wooden oxen and flowing horses before them, they swept away as swiftly as the wind.
Guo Huai cried out in terror, “The gods must surely be aiding them!”
At the sight, every soldier was struck with fear and awe, and none dared give chase.

p.src: Meanwhile, when Sima Yi heard that the forces at the Northern Plain had been defeated, he hastily led an army to their aid in person. He had gone only halfway when a cannon suddenly boomed, and two forces charged out from rugged ground, their battle cries shaking the earth. Upon their banners were written in large characters: “Han Generals Zhang Yi and Liao Hua.” Sima Yi was greatly alarmed at the sight. The Wei troops panicked and fled in every direction. Thus it was said:
